pages.title: Accordion
pages.description: Expand and collapse sections of content An Accordion component is a UI element that allows users to expand and collapse sections of content. It is commonly used to organize information in a compact and accessible manner, displaying only the headers by default and revealing the associated content when clicked. This helps improve the readability of complex or lengthy information by reducing clutter on the page.

pages.title: Alert
pages.description: Success, warning and error messages at a glance An Alert component is a UI element used to display important messages or notifications to users. It can convey different types of information such as success, warning, error, or informational messages, typically styled with distinct colors and icons to highlight the message's significance. Alerts are often used to grab the user's attention and provide immediate feedback on actions or events.

pages.title: Avatar
pages.description: User photos with initials as a fallback An Avatar component shows a person or entity as a small image, with initials or an icon standing in when there is no picture to show. Avatars identify the author of a comment, the owner of a file or the member of a team, in a shape that stays recognisable at any size.

pages.title: Avatar Group
pages.description: Stacked avatars for teams and members An Avatar Group stacks several avatars into one overlapping row and collapses the rest into a count. It answers "who is on this?" in the space of a single line, and is the usual way to show the members of a team, the people on a call or the collaborators on a document.

pages.title: Badge
pages.description: Counts and status markers on any element A Badge component is a small UI element used to display a count, status, or label associated with another element, such as an icon or button. Badges are commonly used to highlight notifications, messages, or any relevant information in a compact and visually distinct way, often appearing as small circles or rectangles with numbers or text.

pages.title: Breadcrumbs
pages.description: Show users where they are in your app A Breadcrumbs component shows where the current page sits in a hierarchy and gives a way back up it. Each entry but the last is a link to an ancestor, which makes a deep section navigable without reaching for the browser's back button.

pages.title: Button
pages.description: Accessible buttons in every variant and size A Button component is a fundamental UI element that allows users to trigger actions or events, such as submitting a form, opening a dialog, or navigating to another page. Buttons are interactive and typically styled to stand out, making it easy for users to identify and interact with them. They can come in various types, such as primary, secondary, or disabled, depending on their purpose or state.

pages.title: Button Group
pages.description: Related actions grouped into one control A Button Group component is a UI element that groups multiple buttons together, allowing users to select from a set of related actions or options. It helps organize buttons in a compact, cohesive layout, typically displayed in a horizontal or vertical row. Button Groups are useful for actions that are closely related or mutually exclusive, providing a clean and structured way to present multiple controls.

pages.title: Calendar
pages.description: An accessible month view for picking dates A Calendar component lays a month out as a grid and lets a date be picked from it. Unlike a date picker it is always open, which suits a booking screen, an availability view or anywhere the surrounding dates are part of the decision.

pages.title: Card
pages.description: Group related content and actions A Card component is a versatile UI element used to display content in a structured and visually appealing way. It typically contains related information, such as text, images, buttons, and other elements, within a bordered or shadowed container. Cards are often used for presenting individual items, like products, articles, or profiles, making the content easy to scan and interact with.

pages.title: Checkbox
pages.description: Accessible checkboxes for forms and lists A Checkbox component is a UI element that allows users to select or deselect one or more options from a list. It typically appears as a small square that can be checked (ticked) or unchecked. Checkboxes are often used in forms, settings, or filters where multiple selections are needed, and they provide a clear, binary choice for users.

pages.title: Checkbox Group
pages.description: Pick several options from one list A Checkbox Group ties several checkboxes to one value, so a set of independent choices is read and written as a single array. It keeps the group's label, its layout and its disabled state in one place instead of spread across the individual boxes.

pages.title: Chip
pages.description: Compact labels for tags, filters and choices A Chip is a compact label for a piece of metadata — a status, a version, a category. It carries a colour and a variant so several chips in a row can be told apart at a glance, and it is deliberately quieter than a badge used for counts.

pages.title: Confirm Alert
pages.description: Ask users to confirm before they act A Confirm Alert component is a UI element that prompts users to confirm or cancel an action before proceeding. It typically displays a message asking for confirmation, along with "Confirm" and "Cancel" buttons, ensuring that the user consciously approves or rejects the action, often used for critical tasks like deletions or irreversible changes.

pages.title: Date Field
pages.description: Type a date segment by segment A Date Field takes a date typed in segments — day, month, year — with no calendar attached. Each segment validates on its own and can be stepped with the arrow keys, which makes it faster than a picker for a date somebody already knows.

pages.title: Date Picker
pages.description: Pick a date from a calendar popover A Date Picker component is a UI element that allows users to select a date from a calendar popup. It provides an intuitive interface for choosing dates with support for date ranges, min/max constraints, and various granularity levels.

pages.title: Date Range Picker
pages.description: Pick a start and end date in one control A Date Range Picker takes a start and an end date in one control, either typed into its segments or chosen from the calendar it opens. Reporting periods, stays and filters all need two dates that make sense together, which is what a range picker enforces.

pages.title: Dialog
pages.description: Modal dialogs for focused tasks A Dialog component is a UI element that displays a pop-up window over the main content to capture user attention or request input. It is often used for tasks like confirmations, alerts, forms, or other interactions that require user feedback before proceeding. Dialogs can include buttons like "OK" or "Cancel" to confirm or dismiss actions, and typically block interaction with the underlying content until closed.

pages.title: Disclosure
pages.description: Show and hide a section of content A Disclosure is one collapsible section: a heading that opens and closes the content under it. It is the single-section counterpart to an accordion, for hiding detail that most readers will not need without sending them to another page for it.

pages.title: Divider
pages.description: Separate content with a clean line A Divider component is a simple UI element used to separate content within a layout, creating visual distinction between sections. It helps enhance the organization and readability of the interface by providing clear boundaries between different elements, such as text blocks, images, or other components. Dividers can be styled in various ways (solid, dashed, or dotted) and can vary in thickness and color to match the overall design of the application.

pages.title: Empty State
pages.description: Guide users when there is nothing to show An Empty State fills a list, table or panel that has nothing in it yet, with a title, an explanation and the action that would change that. A blank area reads as a broken screen; an empty state reads as a screen waiting for its first item.

pages.title: Infinite Scroll
pages.description: Load more content as users scroll An Infinite Scroll component is a user interface feature that automatically loads and displays additional content as the user scrolls down a page. Instead of traditional pagination, this component creates a seamless browsing experience by continuously appending new items, such as images or articles, when the user reaches the bottom of the viewport. This enhances user engagement and keeps the content flow uninterrupted, making it ideal for applications like social media feeds, product galleries, and news websites.

pages.title: Input
pages.description: Text fields with labels and validation An Input component is a user interface element that allows users to enter data, such as text, numbers, or selections. It typically includes various types, such as text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and dropdowns, providing flexibility for different data types. Input components are essential for forms and interactive applications, enabling users to submit information effectively and efficiently.

pages.title: Input OTP
pages.description: One-time passcode entry, digit by digit An Input OTP takes a one-time code as a row of single-character slots, moving focus along as the code is typed or pasted. It is the control used for two-factor sign-in, email verification and anything else that arrives as a short numeric code.

pages.title: Keyboard Key
pages.description: Show keyboard shortcuts in your UI A Keyboard Key renders a key or a shortcut the way a keyboard shows it, so instructions can name a key without quoting it as prose. It is the small styled block you see in a shortcut list, a tooltip or an empty state that suggests a command.

pages.title: Link
pages.description: Accessible links for any destination A Link component is a UI element that allows users to navigate from one page or section to another within a web application or website. Typically styled as underlined text or buttons, links provide a clear indication of interactivity. They can point to internal or external resources and often include features like hover effects or icons to enhance user experience and accessibility.

pages.title: Linkify
pages.description: Turn URLs in plain text into links A Linkify component is a UI tool that automatically detects and converts plain text URLs within a content area into clickable hyperlinks. This enhances user experience by allowing easy access to external resources without the need for manual formatting. Linkify typically recognizes various URL formats and ensures that they are presented in a visually distinct manner, making navigation seamless and intuitive.

pages.title: List Box
pages.description: Selectable lists with keyboard navigation A List Box shows a set of options as a list that can be selected with the mouse or the keyboard, one at a time or several at once. Unlike a select it stays open, which suits a picker built into a panel, a file list or a settings column.

pages.title: Loading
pages.description: Spinners for pages, buttons and sections A Loading component is a UI element that indicates to users that a process is ongoing, such as data fetching, page loading, or background tasks. It typically features visual indicators like spinners, progress bars, or animated icons to convey that the application is busy and to enhance the user experience by preventing confusion or frustration during waiting periods.

pages.title: Dropdown Menu
pages.description: Menus of actions behind one trigger A Dropdown Menu component is a UI element that allows users to select an option from a list that appears when the user clicks or hovers over a button or link. This component helps save space on the interface by displaying additional options only when needed. Dropdown menus are commonly used for navigation, settings, or forms, enabling users to choose from multiple choices in a clean and organized manner.

pages.title: Meter
pages.description: Show a value within a known range A Meter component is a UI element that visually represents a scalar measurement within a known range, such as disk usage, battery level, or CPU load. It provides an at-a-glance indicator of how a value compares to its min and max thresholds.

pages.title: Number Field
pages.description: Numeric input with increment and decrement A Number Field component is a UI element that allows users to enter and adjust numeric values using increment and decrement buttons or direct input. It supports features like min/max constraints, step values, and number formatting.

pages.title: Pagination
pages.description: Move through pages of results A Pagination component walks through a result set page by page, showing the current page, its neighbours and the ends of the range with an ellipsis in between. It keeps a long list navigable without loading all of it at once.

pages.title: Popover
pages.description: Floating content anchored to a trigger A Popover component is a UI element that displays additional information or actions when users interact with a specific trigger, such as a button or link. It typically appears as a small overlay or tooltip that provides context, tips, or options without navigating away from the current page. Popovers enhance user experience by offering relevant content in a concise format while maintaining focus on the main interface.

pages.title: Progress
pages.description: Show how far a task has come A Progress component visually indicates the completion status of a task or process. It typically consists of a progress bar that fills up as the task progresses, providing users with a clear and immediate understanding of how much of the task is completed and how much remains. This component is commonly used in forms, uploads, downloads, and loading states to enhance user experience by managing expectations and keeping users informed.

pages.title: Progress Circle
pages.description: Circular progress for tasks and uploads A Progress Circle shows how far along a task is as a ring rather than a bar, which fits a tile, a button or a dense row where a full-width bar would not. Left without a value it spins as an indeterminate indicator.

pages.title: Radio Group
pages.description: Pick exactly one option from a set A Radio Group component is a UI element that allows users to select one option from a set of mutually exclusive choices. It typically consists of multiple radio buttons, where only one button can be selected at a time. Radio groups are commonly used in forms to gather user preferences, ensuring a clear and organized way to present options for selection. They enhance user experience by providing a straightforward interface for making single-choice decisions.

pages.title: Scroll Shadow
pages.description: Fade the edges to hint at more content A Scroll Shadow fades the edges of a scrollable area while there is more content beyond them, so a cut-off list looks scrollable instead of finished. The shadows appear and disappear as the content is scrolled, on either axis.

pages.title: Select
pages.description: Pick one option from a dropdown list A Select or ComboBox component is a UI element that allows users to choose one or more options from a dropdown list. It typically displays a default value or prompt, and when clicked, it expands to show a list of available choices. Users can either select an option from the list or, in the case of a ComboBox, input custom values. This component is ideal for conserving space in forms and making it easy for users to make selections quickly.

pages.title: Search Field
pages.description: A text field built for search queries A Search Field component is a UI element that provides a text input specifically designed for search functionality. It includes a built-in search icon and clear button, allowing users to quickly enter, modify, and clear search queries.

pages.title: Sheet
pages.description: Panels that slide in from the edge A Sheet component is a UI element that presents content in a sliding panel, often overlaying the main application interface. It is typically used for displaying additional information, forms, or actions without navigating away from the current view. Sheets can be swiped or tapped to expand or collapse, providing a clean and efficient way to manage user interactions and maintain focus on the main content.

pages.title: Skeleton
pages.description: Placeholder shapes while content loads A Skeleton component is a placeholder UI element that represents the layout of content before it loads. It typically features a grey or light-colored shape mimicking the structure of the actual content (such as text blocks, images, or buttons) to indicate that loading is in progress. Skeleton components enhance user experience by providing a visual cue that content is being fetched, reducing perceived loading times and preventing layout shifts.

pages.title: Slider
pages.description: Pick a value by dragging a handle A Slider component is a UI element that allows users to select a value from a range by sliding a handle along a track. It provides an interactive way to adjust settings, such as volume, brightness, or other continuous values, with smooth transitions. Sliders can be single or multi-valued, enabling users to make precise selections visually, enhancing the overall user experience.

pages.title: Switch
pages.description: Turn a setting on or off A Switch component is a UI element that allows users to toggle between two states, typically representing an on/off or enabled/disabled choice. It is visually represented as a sliding toggle or checkbox and provides immediate feedback when the user interacts with it. Switch components are commonly used for settings, preferences, and feature activations in applications, enhancing user experience by simplifying the selection process.

pages.title: Switch Group
pages.description: Several on/off settings in one group A Switch Group collects several switches under one label and one value, for a screen of settings that are each on or off. Every row names its setting and carries its own switch, and the group reports the set that is currently on.

pages.title: Table
pages.description: Show rows of data in clear columns A Table component is a structured UI element that organizes and displays data in rows and columns, making it easy to read and compare information. Tables can include features like sorting, filtering, pagination, and inline editing, allowing users to interact with the data efficiently. They are commonly used to present datasets, such as user information, product listings, or any structured content that benefits from a grid-like layout.

pages.title: Tag Group
pages.description: A set of tags users can select A Tag Group component is a UI element that displays a collection of tags or labels, allowing users to select, filter, or remove tags. It supports multiple selection modes and removable tags, making it ideal for categorization, filtering, and labeling interfaces.

pages.title: Tabs
pages.description: Switch between views in one place A Tabs component is a UI element that allows users to switch between different views or sections of content within the same interface. Organized as a series of labeled tabs, this component enhances navigation by displaying only one section at a time, helping to reduce clutter and improve user experience. Users can easily access various related content or features by clicking on the respective tabs, making it ideal for dashboards, settings pages, or any multi-section layout.

pages.title: Textarea
pages.description: Multi-line text input for longer answers A Textarea component is an input field that allows users to enter multi-line text. It provides a larger area for text input compared to a standard text input field, making it ideal for comments, feedback, or any scenario where users need to provide detailed information. Textareas can be resized, styled, and configured to support features like character limits, placeholders, and auto-resizing to enhance user experience.

pages.title: Time Field
pages.description: Type a time segment by segment A Time Field takes a time typed in segments — hour, minute, and the period where the locale uses one. It reads and writes a time value rather than a string, so a schedule or a reminder gets a value it can compare and store.

pages.title: Toast
pages.description: Brief notifications that dismiss themselves A Toast component is a transient notification that appears on the screen to provide feedback or information to users without interrupting their workflow. Typically displayed at the top or bottom of the screen, toasts are brief messages that automatically disappear after a short duration. They are commonly used to inform users about actions such as successful submissions, updates, or alerts, enhancing the overall user experience with minimal disruption.

pages.title: Toggle Button
pages.description: A button that stays pressed A Toggle Button is a button that stays pressed, for a setting that belongs on a toolbar rather than in a form — bold, italic, mute, pin. It reports its state through its appearance, so a row of them reads as the current formatting.

pages.title: Toolbar
pages.description: Group related controls in one bar A Toolbar groups the controls that act on the thing below it and makes them one stop on the keyboard: arrow keys move between the controls, so a row of buttons is reached with one Tab rather than several. It can be laid out in a row or a column, joined or spaced.

pages.title: Tooltip
pages.description: Short hints on hover and focus A Tooltip component is a small, informative pop-up that appears when a user hovers over or focuses on an element, such as a button or icon. It provides additional context or explanations about that element without cluttering the interface. Tooltips enhance user experience by offering helpful hints, instructions, or details, ensuring that information is accessible without overwhelming the layout.

pages.description: Start from the games example in the Nayan UI repo and see how its Car Racing is built. Start from the example What is in the project How Car Racing is built 1. Load the car 2. It holds one complete game, Car Racing, that runs on iOS, Android and the web from the same code. The CLI copies it for you. It is the same Car Racing as in Playtura and on nayanui.com/games. The only change is the car, which is loaded from glTF files instead of built in code. Three parts. shared/ holds the game, written once in React Native. mobile/ is an Expo app that renders it. web/ is a Vite app that renders the same component through react-native-web. Car Racing is seven files in shared/src/games/car-racing. The rules have no React, the scene only draws, and the screen connects them to the shared game screen.

pages.title: React Quickstart
pages.description: Mount a scene in a React web app. Write the scene Mount it Next.js and Vite Keep the scene in plain functions so React only mounts it. useWorld calls setupScene once with a fresh world after the engine loads, and builds a new one when its deps change. useWorld returns null until the world is ready and passes start-up failures, such as the WebAssembly failing to load, to onError. GameView needs a container with a real height; paused stops updates and drawing but keeps the world. In the Next.js App Router, mark the screen "use client" and load it with dynamic(..., { ssr: false }) so worlds are only created in the browser. In Vite, mount it with createRoot(root).render(<Game />); React Native Web isn't needed.

pages.title: React Native Quickstart
pages.description: Mount a scene in a React Native development build. Write the scene Mount it Pause when the screen loses focus Keep the scene in plain functions so React only mounts it. useWorld calls setupScene once with a fresh world after the engine loads, and builds a new one when its deps change. useWorld returns null until the world is ready and passes start-up failures to onError, such as a missing native module in Expo Go. paused stops updates and drawing but keeps the world. pages.title: Common Recipes
pages.description: Short, copyable solutions for everyday game tasks. Move without React state Fall and bounce Steer with a joystick Jump only when grounded Pick up on contact Tap to recolor Chase the player Pop and remove Show the score in React Delay in game time Build a model once, spawn it many times Sound and haptics on an action Confetti on a win Face the movement direction Queue per-frame moves on world.transforms from onUpdate; they apply in one native call when GameView steps the world. Each recipe returning a function is meant to be called from onUpdate. A fixed floor and a dynamic ball: physics handles gravity and the bounce. useJoystick returns a mutable state: read it in onUpdate, never mirror it into React state. groundVelocity sets X/Z speed and keeps gravity.

pages.title: AI Agent Guide
pages.description: Rules, file layout, API choices and a template for coding agents. Read first File structure One API per task Never do Game template Agent prompt Verify Start from /engine.json and the first game; check every name in the API reference. Never guess names from another engine. Rules live in plain TypeScript with no UI imports, so one file serves web and native. The hook owns the world; the screen owns layout and GameView. Each task has one way. Use it.

pages.title: World & Entities
pages.description: Own a world, spawn and change entities, and dispose them safely. Lifecycle in five rules Spawn, set and despawn EntityOptions reference Rotations with quat Per-frame moves with world.transforms Parents and groups Queries, bounds and gravity Reset and dispose useWorld and GameView make a complete scene; these five rules keep it leak-free and crash-free. 1. Own the world with useWorld(capacity, setup), or create it in an effect after await warmUpEngine(); never during render or at module scope. 2. GameView steps the world right after onUpdate; call world.update(dt) yourself only to step differently, and GameView then skips its step (it watches world.updateCount). 3. Queue per-frame moves on world.transforms in onUpdate; the step applies them, so call flush() only before reading positions back. 4. Dispose the world on unmount (useWorld does) and release your subscriptions with it. 5. Check world.isDisposed instead of keeping a flag: afterwards set, despawn, has, animate, stopAnimation, impulse, clips, timers, queries and forEachCollision are no-ops, while spawn and update throw.

pages.title: GameView
pages.description: Draw a world, run the frame loop, choose quality and layer overlays. GameView props Frames and dt Render quality Frame statistics Overlays Pause GameView draws a RenderSource (usually a World) and calls onUpdate once a frame. Other props are read live; changing source restarts the view. On iOS and Android frames come from the display clock at 60 Hz: onUpdate steps the game and hands a copy to the engine's render thread, so JavaScript never waits on the GPU. A frame not yet drawn is replaced by a newer one, not queued; the web uses requestAnimationFrame. dt is capped at 0.1 s and is 0 until the first frame is on screen, so intros don't play unseen. Step the world yourself only for a different dt, such as slow motion. auto starts at high and steps down only while drawing can't keep up: after one second under ~33 fps, or a few seconds missing ~50 fps. It drops shadow detail first, then MSAA, then resolution, and climbs back after about ten smooth seconds. Quality can't fix a slow game loop; that shows in updateMs, not renderMs. The chosen level survives pauses and only restarts with a new source.

pages.title: Camera & Lighting
pages.description: Aim, follow and shake the camera, and light and color the scene. Perspective and orthographic Follow and shake Directional light Background and fog Flat boards with frontLight Colors and toColor A Camera has mutable eye and target tuples and a vertical fov in radians. ortho (half the visible height in world units) makes it orthographic and overrides fov. Mutate the object from onUpdate; GameView reads it every frame. Keep a tiny offset for straight-down views so eye and target never align vertically. camera.follow = { target, offset, smoothing? } eases the target toward the entity's drawn position and keeps the eye at offset. smoothing is roughly the catch-up time in seconds (default 0.15, 0 is rigid); null returns control. camera.shake is a strength in world units that fades by itself. One directional light with ambient fill and a shadow map centred on the camera target. A small shadowExtent clips distant shadows; a large one blurs them.

pages.title: Physics & Collisions
pages.description: Add rigid bodies, sensors, layers, impulses and raycasts. Bodies and colliders PhysicsOptions reference Steer and push Sensors, layers and masks Collision events Raycasts Impact feedback dynamic bodies move under gravity and contact, kinematic ones are moved by you and push dynamic ones, and fixed ones never move. The collider matches the mesh (models get a box) and is sized from the entity when the body is created. Later scale changes don't resize it, so set explicit sizes for gameplay volumes. set(entity, { physics: null }) removes the body. physics takes a BodyType string for defaults, or PhysicsOptions. groundVelocity sets horizontal [x, z] speed and keeps the vertical one, so a steered body still falls. impulse(entity, vec) is a one-off push for dynamic bodies: jumps, knockback.

pages.title: Animation
pages.description: Tween, keyframe and spring entities in Rust, awaiting their completion. Animate and await AnimateOptions reference Keyframes and paths Groups and stagger Springs Stop animations world.animate(targets, to, options?) runs in Rust and returns a promise that resolves when every part finishes, is replaced or stopped, or its entity or world goes. Resolution means it ended, not that it reached the target. Each property runs on its own channel, so a piece can move while it pulses; animating a property again replaces only that one. A repeat: "forever" promise resolves only when stopped, replaced or despawned, so never await it. Pass an array of up to 64 Keyframes to pass through values in order. Each may set at (0..1 of the duration; default evenly spaced), and path: "smooth" curves through them.

pages.title: Skeletal Animation
pages.description: Play GLB clips per character, crossfade them and ground feet on the animated pose. Load a rig and read its clips Play, hold, crossfade and stop Ground feet on the animated pose loadModel resolves a LoadedModel whose animations list each clip's name and duration in seconds; jointCount is 0 for a static mesh. Read clip names from the asset instead of assuming one called walk. Skins hold up to 128 joints. Every entity spawned from the model has its own clip player, so characters sharing a model animate independently. world.playClip(entity, name, options) switches to a clip, crossfading from the current pose, and returns false if it can't play. Re-selecting the playing clip only changes its speed; pass time to seek. Hold a ready-screen pose with time: 0 and speed: 0, then play on Start. stopClip(entity) freezes the current pose and stopClip(entity, true) returns to the bind pose. world.sampleSkinnedVertices(entity, indices, out, after) writes model-space XYZ for chosen vertex indices into out (three floats each) and returns false when it can't sample. Reuse both arrays and query a few boot vertices of your asset; never skin the whole character in JS. In onUpdate, pass the frame's dt as after: the world steps by it right afterwards, so you read the pose about to be drawn. Scale and transform samples by the actor before comparing them with terrain.

pages.title: Input & Picking
pages.description: Read taps, swipes, drags, pinches, a joystick and browser keys, and map screen points to the world. Tap, swipe and long press Drag and pinch On-screen joystick Pick, project and unproject Browser keyboard input GameView reports onTap(x, y), onSwipe(direction) and onLongPress(x, y) in points from the view's top-left, which are CSS pixels on the web (don't multiply by devicePixelRatio). A long press fires after half a second held still, and no tap follows it. Touches claimed by onOverlayTouch never reach these callbacks, and pausing the view cancels any touch in progress. onDrag receives start, move and end; an end with cancelled means a pinch or the system took the touch, so put a held piece back. onPinch reports two-finger zoom and rotation, and starting one ends any drag. useJoystick() returns a stable { x, y } object that Joystick writes on touch, each axis in -1..1 with y up, without re-rendering React. Read it in onUpdate. The stick is relative: wherever the finger lands in the pad is the centre. Render it beside GameView, not inside it, and position it with style; size is the pad diameter (default 150).

pages.title: Effects & Particles
pages.description: Fire ready-made effects in one call, or shape your own particles with world.burst. Ready-made effects EffectOptions Dust puffs and flashes Pop a cleared piece Custom particles with world.burst Import effects and call one function per event; each layers a few bursts (big slow pieces, small fast ones, a glow, lingering puffs) that move, fade and clean up in Rust. Particles advance with the world, so they pause with the game. Every particle takes a world slot, so size the World's capacity for the busiest moment. Effects throw on a disposed world: check world.isDisposed in callbacks that can run late. confetti, sparkle, shatter, splash, sparks and explosion share EffectOptions; position, colors, size, speed, count and lifetime are required, except colors for explosion. Sizes are world units, speeds units per second and times seconds. effects.dust makes soft puffs that swell and fade; gravity defaults to 0 so dust hangs, and positive values rise like smoke. effects.flash draws one glow at a point; channels above 1 glow, most easily via effects.hot(color).

pages.title: Scoreboards & Timers
pages.description: Track score, lives and time, and schedule delays that pause with the game. Rules and listeners Ready, start and score Scoreboard operations Game-time timers world.scoreboard keeps score, lives and the clock in Rust; read score, best, lives, seconds, shownSeconds and running. Assign handlers for the game's rules and call listen for UI that follows along: it adds handlers without replacing others and returns an unlisten function. Callbacks run from the world's step only when a value changed, handlers first and then listeners in order. best lasts for the scoreboard's life, so persist personal bests yourself. reset(lives, countdownSeconds) begins a run: score 0, those lives and a stopped clock that already shows the full countdown, which is your ready screen. resume() starts it when the player presses Start; reset actors and input yourself. Operations change state immediately; their callbacks follow on the next step. stop() and resume() affect only the clock, not the rest of the simulation.

pages.title: Audio & Haptics
pages.description: Play sounds through the engine's mixer and add haptics that respect player settings. Load a sound bank Play, loop and stop voices Player settings and autoplay Collision sounds and haptics Haptic taps and patterns audio.load({ name: source }) returns a SoundBank at once; await bank.ready before relying on it, since plays before then are ignored and failed files are logged and skipped. Sounds are WAV (PCM or float, mono or stereo): URLs on the web, require(...) in React Native. Playing returns a Voice (or null); keep it and pass it to audio.stop when leaving. A screen owns its loops and stops them on unmount. Mirror the player's settings onto audio.enabled and haptics.enabled; both are global switches. On the web, output starts on the first click, touch or key press and suspends in hidden tabs.

pages.title: Drawing & Painting
pages.description: Paint with native brushes, layers and undo, and reuse the artwork inside games. Documents and canvases A paint screen with undo Brushes and tools Shapes and fills Layers and the view Save and load Export SVG and PNG Use a drawing as a game texture Paint from game input Read strokes Score what was drawn A DrawingDocument holds the artwork in the Rust core: strokes, layers, tool settings and undo history. DrawingCanvas shows a document and feeds it touch, pencil or mouse input without going through React state. new DrawingDocument(width, height, pixelRatio = 2) takes document units, the coordinates every method uses; await warmUpEngine() first (required on the web). Dispose it on unmount: after that its methods throw, so check isDisposed in late callbacks. Editing methods return the new DrawingState and onChange delivers it after each stroke, so drive buttons from state.canUndo and state.canRedo. undo(), redo() and clear() share one history with strokes and layer edits. setBrush(options) sets the whole brush at once; updateControls(partial) changes single settings (tool, color, width, shape…) and reset: true restores the defaults. Current values are in state.controls.

pages.title: Models & Textures
pages.description: Load glTF models and images in parallel, recover from failures and map textures. Load assets in parallel Errors and retry Models and glTF limits Textures, tint and atlas regions Pass a URL string (or a bundler import) on the web, and require(...) or a URI in React Native; add glb and gltf to Metro's assetExts and install expo-asset for bundled Android release assets. Loaders start the engine themselves and cache by source and options, so a second call returns the same promise. On iOS and Android, loadTexture, loadModel, loadFont and audio.load decode on native background threads, so Promise.all loads a level in parallel while the loading screen animates, and meshes register with the renderer inside Rust. The web's single-threaded core decodes on the main thread, so load before play, never in onUpdate. A failed load rejects with an Error naming the loader and source (loadTexture: couldn't load …), with the original error as cause. Failures aren't cached, so calling the loader again retries; a file the core rejects discards its saved bytes, while network and start-up failures keep them. Offer a Retry action rather than retrying from onUpdate, and ignore results that arrive after unmount. loadModel reads glTF 2.0: a .glb, or a .gltf with embedded buffers; external buffer files are rejected, so export a self-contained GLB. It keeps meshes, node transforms, vertex and material colors, one base-color texture per model, skins and clips, and decodes EXT_meshopt_compression, but it isn't a general importer for every material extension. Every entity using a model draws in one instanced call, and colliders sized from it fit its bounding box. Ship third-party models with their licences.

pages.title: Text & Fonts
pages.description: Load fonts, then draw, update and measure 3D text. Load a font Spawn and update text Measure text loadFont(source, options) reads TrueType or OpenType outlines and builds a mesh per glyph; prewarm known characters with chars, and others build on first use. Characters the font lacks draw as ?, and there's no complex shaping, color emoji or fallback font. Source, depth and weight identify a shared font; a later call with other chars only adds glyphs. Font licences still apply. Spawn an entity with text and font; letters are 1 unit tall at scale 1 and the line is a single row. Setting text again reuses the existing letter entities. Each drawn letter is a child entity that counts against the World's capacity. Text is lit, shadowed geometry in a scene, and flat and unlit in an overlay. measureText(font, text, layout) returns a line's advance in ems, with the same glyph loading, spacing and fallbacks as drawing; multiply by the entity's scale for world units. Pass the letterSpacing and tabular you draw with.

pages.title: Procedural Geometry
pages.description: Build meshes in code from paths, profiles, tubes and merged parts. Geometry and createShape Paths and extrusion Lathe profiles Tubes Merge parts, recolor and smooth Builders return Geometry: a Float32Array of 11 floats per vertex (position, normal, RGB color, UV) and a Uint32Array of triangle indices. createShape(geometry, options) registers it as a Model for any entity's mesh, and equal geometry and options reuse the same model. Mesh ids are app-wide and never freed (about 4,080), so build each mesh once after warmUpEngine (useWorld's setup runs after it), keep it at module scope and spawn many entities from it. shapeGeometry(name, { color }) copies a built-in shape (cube, sphere, plane, cylinder, cone, capsule, torus, roundedBox) for merging. Path builds 2D outlines like SVG (x right, y down, world units) with chaining methods, and Path.fromSVG parses path data (M L H V C S Q T A Z, absolute and relative). extrude(path, options) fills it into a solid facing +Z, flipped so it stands as drawn. depth defaults to 0.2, and 0 gives a one-sided flat face. fillRule defaults to nonzero; evenodd makes every inner contour a hole. lathe(profile, options) spins a profile around the Y axis, like a potter's wheel: a Path (x is the radius, y down) or [radius, height] points. Open ends away from the axis are capped, and a sweep below 2π closes its cut faces too. Make displace equal at u = 0 and 1 to avoid a seam. Color callbacks paint vertices, so more segments, capRings or cutSteps give finer patterns at a vertex cost.

pages.title: Surfaces & Lofts
pages.description: Sample parametric surfaces, loft smooth bodies and sculpt geometry. Parametric surfaces Lofts, blocks and ellipsoids Smooth curves and deformation parametricSurface(sample, options) turns (u, v) from 0 to 1 into positions, for terrain, cloth, wings and ribbons. Triangles wind by dP/du × dP/dv, so order coordinates so the front faces outward. loft(sections, options) runs a smooth closed body through rounded-rectangle cross-sections along Z: vehicle shells, cabins, shoes. It needs at least two sections in strictly increasing or decreasing z. block(w, h, d, square = 6, color?) is a rounded box with flat end caps, and ellipsoid(radii, color?, around = 16) an exact ellipsoid. All three return Geometry to merge or deform before createShape. smoothCurve(points) returns a smooth Hermite function through increasing [x, value] points, clamped past the ends, for profiles and tuning curves. deformGeometry(geometry, (position, uv) => Vec3) moves every vertex of a copy and recomputes its normals. Deform smooth surfaces before adding hard-edged parts; it can't change a registered model or keep a rig.

pages.title: Solid Modelling
pages.description: Model solids in code, then optimize them and prepare LOD levels. Build a solid Tessellate, inspect and deform Optimize and build LOD levels A Solid is an immutable recipe: every operation returns a new Solid. Primitives are centred at the origin, and cylinders and tori stand on the Y axis. createSolid(solid, options) tessellates, optimizes and registers the recipe once, then returns the same model for the same recipe. Call it after warmUpEngine, during setup; paint takes 0..1 tuples, and white parts can be tinted per entity. solidGeometry(solid, { resolution, uv }) returns editable, unregistered Geometry: resolution is 8..128 cells across the longest side (default 48) and uv picks the planar projection 'xy' (default), 'xz' or 'yz'. Cost grows roughly cubically with resolution, so build during setup, never in onUpdate. getGeometryStats reports vertices, triangles, bytes and bounds without registering anything. deformGeometry(geometry, (position, uv) => newPosition) sculpts a copy of one smooth surface and recomputes its normals. optimizeGeometry(geometry, { ratio, error, lockBorders }) returns a cleaned copy: ratio 1 (default) only welds and reorders, lower ratios simplify within error (default 0.001), and lockBorders (default true) keeps open edges fixed. Use it on static opaque meshes only, never on skinned meshes or geometry whose vertex indices other code reads. createGeometryLods(geometry, ratios = [1, 0.5, 0.25], options) simplifies the original independently per level. There is no automatic LOD switch: register the levels once and swap an entity's mesh when its distance changes.

pages.title: Cache & Performance
pages.description: Let the engine cache assets, keep frames allocation-free and spread heavy work over frames. Automatic asset caching Clear saved assets Cache expensive factories Move many entities with world.transforms Zero-allocation frames Frames and threads Culling and background decoding Slice long setup with afterNextFrame Practical budgets You don't need an app cache: each file downloads and decodes once per session, equal geometry shares one registration, and prepared meshes are saved for later launches. Records never expire and aren't evicted; full or denied storage falls back to memory, and corrupt records rebuild. Disposing a world keeps loaded handles valid. Change the URL (for example ?v=2) when a file's contents change. clearAssetCache() removes saved geometry, original files and temporary download bytes; call it only from a user action. It rejects when storage can't be cleared, live worlds and handles keep working, and custom ProceduralStorage adapters are left alone. new ProceduralCache(revision) saves what a deterministic factory returns (models, arrays and JSON values): get(key, build) restores or builds and saves, and peek(key) restores without building (undefined when missing). Use one revision per game and prefix keys with its folder, so an update rebuilds only that game's records. The engine's store checksums records in Rust (ProceduralStorage.verified), so restores skip the JS checksum; a custom storage without verified keeps it. stats counts hits and builds, flush() awaits pending writes, and worlds, entities, textures and imported rigs never belong in it.

pages.title: RenderSource
pages.description: Draw your own simulation with GameView through the instance-buffer contract. Instance buffer contract Stepping and the view Draw it with GameView A RenderSource packs instances grouped by mesh: matrices holds a column-major mat4 each, colors an RGBA each, and optional regions a texture rectangle each, in the same order. Only the first count instances draw; capacity sizes the GPU buffers. ranges holds [first, count] per mesh id: opaque instances at ranges[2 * mesh], transparent ones at ranges[2 * (MAX_MESHES + mesh)]. Meshes must already be registered (built-ins after warmUpEngine, createShape or a loader). GameView calls source.update(dt) after onUpdate each frame, unless its updateCount changed during onUpdate or isDisposed is true. setView(viewProj, width, height) receives the camera of each drawn frame for your own picking. A custom source gets no physics, timers, animation or picking from World, and nativeWorld belongs only to a real World. Prefer World unless you already own a simulation. Await warmUpEngine so the built-in meshes exist, then pass the source to GameView with a Camera and Light, like a world. A custom source can also be GameView's overlay.

pages.description: Find the fix for common engine problems, then check a build before shipping. Setup and rendering Worlds, frames and queries Assets, animation and feedback Production checklist Most blank screens are a missing native build, an unawaited warm-up or a view with no size. Log onError first. After dispose, cleanup calls and queries are no-ops, but spawn, update, burst and effects throw. Check world.isDisposed after every await before spawning. When a clip or asset fails, print what the model actually contains before changing code.
